# Abstract

Sri Lanka and the Maldives archipelago (encompassing 63.718 km² across 768 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells) accommodated one of the most sophisticated hydraulic agrarian civilisations and maritime networks in the Indian Ocean basin. Stretching from the dry zone northern lowlands of Rajarata, drained by the seasonal Malvathu Oya and perennial Mahaweli Ganga, across the Miocene limestone shelf of the Jaffna peninsula, the equatorial rain forests and granite highlands of the southwest wet zone and the semi-arid river basins of Ruhuna, to the dispersed oceanic atolls of the Maldives, the region developed distinctive socio-ecological systems. In Sri Lanka, human settlement combined village-scale tank cascades, monumental trans-basin canal diversions, terraced hill paddy cultivation and coastal emporia. In the Maldives, insular populations adapted to miniature coral islets through pelagic tuna fisheries, coconut agroforestry and the harvesting of cowrie shells (*Monetaria moneta*) that circulated as universal currency across Afro-Eurasia.

Reconstructed across five physiographic and historical divisions from 10000BC to 1796AD under INDUS, regional population expanded from 12k terminal Pleistocene and early Holocene foragers in 10000BC during initial Mesolithic cave and dune occupation to 65k in 3000BC as microlithic hunter-gatherers exploited lowland ecotones. Demographic expansion quickened during the first millennium BC with the introduction of iron metallurgy, megalithic cist cemeteries, horse husbandry and tank irrigation, reaching 280k by 500BC and 650k by 0AD. Under the classical hydraulic kingdom of Anuradhapura, population doubled to 1,2M in 500AD and expanded to 1,75M by 1000AD as sophisticated valve-pit (*bisokotuwa*) engineering permitted the impoundment of colossal storage reservoirs. Population attained an all-time pre-colonial zenith of 1,95M inhabitants in 1200AD (yielding an aggregate regional density of 30,6 persons per km² or 3.060,36 persons per 100 km²) during the Polonnaruwa climax under Parakramabahu I.

Following Chola military incursions, the thirteenth-century breakdown of dry zone canal maintenance, malaria infestation and the geopolitical fragmentation of the hydraulic core, demographic mass shifted southward and westward. Regional population contracted to 1,55M by 1500AD (-20,5% across three centuries) as populations abandoned the malarial lowlands of Rajarata and resettled within rain-fed wet zone valleys (Dambadeniya, Yapahuwa, Kurunegala, Gampola, Kotte) and the Kandyan montane massif, while independent Tamil principalities consolidated across the Jaffna peninsula and the Vanni forests. Maritime commerce quickened following Portuguese (1505AD) and Dutch (1658AD) fort construction along coastal harbours (Colombo, Galle, Jaffna, Trincomalee). By 1700AD regional numbers recovered to 1,75M, rising to 1,98M by 1796AD on the eve of British annexation of Dutch maritime possessions.

Demographic mass followed shifting ecological and administrative poles. At the 1200AD apex, Kotte and the Kandyan wet zone supported 741k people (38% of regional population; 30,34 persons per km²), the Rajarata hydraulic core housed 585k inhabitants (30%; 24,81 persons per km²), Ruhuna and the eastern littoral sustained 273k (14%; 18,18 persons per km²), the Jaffna peninsula supported 273k (14%; attaining the highest agrarian density at 402,06 persons per km²), and the Maldives archipelago housed 78k (4%; 3.120 persons per km² on coral land). By 1796AD, the wet zone and Kandyan highlands accommodated 752,4k inhabitants (38%), Rajarata supported 594k (30%), Ruhuna housed 277,2k (14%), Jaffna accommodated 277,2k (14%), and the Maldives atolls housed 79,2k (4%). This historical demographic synthesis links 1.642 catalogued settlement trajectories with systematic geoarchaeological surveys of reservoir siltation, speleothem climate proxies, epigraphic tank donations and colonial cadastral rolls (*tombos*), providing an archaeological baseline for insular demographic evolution in southern South Asia.

# Background

## Environmental Gradients and Monsoonal Climatology

The physical geography of Sri Lanka and the Maldives is governed by marked climatic and geological contrasts across the Indian Ocean equatorial belt [@Manogaran1987Ethnic; @Arachchige2021Multi]. Sri Lanka covers 65.610 km² of land area, rising from broad coastal plains to a central highland massif exceeding 2.500 metres in elevation (Pidurutalagala, 2.524 m). The island is divided into two primary climatic domains by its central mountains: the southwest wet zone and the surrounding dry zone [@Abeywardana2018Ancient; @Sutcliffe2011Historical].

The southwest wet zone receives heavy precipitation from both the southwest monsoon (Yala, May to September) and the northeast monsoon (Maha, October to January), yielding annual rainfall totals between 2.500 mm and 5.000 mm [@Arachchige2021Multi]. Rain-fed drainage networks, including the Kelani Ganga, Kalu Ganga and Gin Ganga, maintain perennial streamflow through dense tropical rainforests and deeply incised valleys [@Hewawasam2022Traditiona].

In contrast, the dry zone, comprising nearly two-thirds of the island across northern, north-central and southeastern plains, receives rainfall almost exclusively during the northeast monsoon (October to January), averaging 1.000 mm to 1.500 mm annually [@Abeywardana2018Ancient; @Bebermeier2023Domesticat]. The subsequent dry season (May to September) brings intense evaporation, desiccating winds and severe water deficits [@Sutcliffe2011Historical]. Rivers such as the Malvathu Oya, Kala Oya and Yan Oya shrink to intermittent trickles during the summer drought [@Dissanayake2022Megalithic]. The Mahaweli Ganga, rising in the central wet highlands, forms the only perennial river traversing the dry plains to debouch at Gokanna (Trincomalee) on the eastern seaboard [@Abeywardana2019Evolution].

The Jaffna peninsula in the extreme north exhibits distinct karst hydrogeology [@Manogaran1987Ethnic]. Devoid of perennial streams, it rests upon porous Miocene limestone where freshwater floats as a shallow Ghyben-Herzberg lens above intrusive sea water. Agriculture in Jaffna relies upon stone-lined wells and lift-irrigation (*tulams*) tapping this fragile groundwater aquifer [@Manogaran1987Ethnic].

Southwest of Sri Lanka, across 600 km of open sea, lies the Maldives archipelago, a double chain of 26 natural atolls resting on the Chagos-Laccadive submarine ridge [@Clark2008Islands; @Feener2021Maldives]. Comprising 1.192 low-lying coral islets totaling only 298 km² of land, the archipelago possesses zero surface streams and negligible soil depth [@MD2023Spatial]. Inhabitants relied upon rainfall harvesting, freshwater lenses floating over subterranean coral limestone, pelagic fishing and coconut agroforestry [@Feener2021Maldives; @Cui2025Religion].

## Prehistoric Foragers and the Mesolithic-Neolithic Horizon

Human habitation in Sri Lanka extends to the late Pleistocene [@Clark2008Islands; @Coningham2025Village]. Microlithic assemblages recovered from cave sites, including Fa Hien-lena, Batadombalena and Kitulgala Beli-lena in the southwest wet zone, date from 38000BC through 10000BC [@Coningham2025Village]. These terminal Pleistocene forager communities hunted arboreal mammals (giant squirrels, monkeys) and gathered wild breadfruit (*Artocarpus*), canarium nuts and edible molluscs, manufacturing geometric quartz microliths, bone projectile points and personal ornaments [@Clark2008Islands].

Along the southeastern and northwestern coasts, Mesolithic foragers occupied coastal sand dunes and lagoon margins (the Iranamadu Formation), exploiting marine fisheries and estuarine shell beds [@Coningham2025Village]. During the early Holocene (10000BC to 3000BC), regional population grew slowly from 12k to 65k inhabitants, constrained by the carrying capacity of rain-forest foraging and littoral harvesting. The Maldives archipelago was visited during this era by transient maritime voyagers, but permanent atoll settlement awaited the development of long-distance sailing craft and reliable deep-sea navigation [@Clark2008Islands; @Feener2021Maldives].

## Megalithic Settlement and Early Historic State Formation

During the early first millennium BC (ca. 1000BC to 500BC), Sri Lanka underwent a profound economic and demographic transformation with the arrival of Early Iron Age cultural elements from peninsular South India [@Dissanayake2022Megalithic; @Coningham2025Village]. This transition was characterised by:
1. Iron pyrotechnology and metal tools, including axes, hoes and billhooks that enabled the clearance of dense dry zone scrub forest.
2. Megalithic burial traditions, encompassing dolmenoid cists, urn interments and stone circles, as documented in the Yan Oya and Deduru Oya river basins [@Dissanayake2022Megalithic].
3. Black and Red Ware (BRW) pottery, shared widely across the Palk Strait and peninsular India.
4. Domesticated zebu cattle, sheep, goats and horses, alongside the introduction of irrigated wet-rice agriculture (*Oryza sativa*).
5. Initial earthen embankments impounding seasonal runoff across shallow dry zone valleys [@Abeywardana2019Evolution; @Bebermeier2023Domesticat].

Stratified excavations at the Anuradhapura Citadel indicate that the protohistoric settlement expanded from a 10 ha village in 800BC to an urban trading town covering over 50 ha by 500BC [@Coningham2025Village; @Bohingamuwa2017Lanka]. Early Brahmi inscriptions scratched on ceramic sherds date to the fifth century BC, documenting early administrative and mercantile literacy [@Coningham2025Village]. Regional population expanded to 280k in 500BC, with demographic gravity shifting toward the dry zone lowlands where small earthen reservoirs enabled dependable rice harvests [@Abeywardana2018Ancient].

## Classical Hydraulic Engineering: Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa

The introduction of Buddhism during the third century BC under King Devanampiya Tissa accelerated urbanisation and monarchical consolidation [@DameronNandan2003World; @Coningham2025Village; @Allchin1995Archaeology]. Over the subsequent fifteen centuries, the dry zone kingdoms of Anuradhapura (437BC to 1017AD) and Polonnaruwa (1070AD to 1232AD) constructed an extraordinary hydraulic landscape that supported rapid demographic expansion [@Abeywardana2018Ancient; @Hawken2021Long].

The cornerstone of this agrarian civilisation was the cascade reservoir system (*ellangawa*) [@Abhayawardana2019Tank; @Bebermeier2023Domesticat; @Sumanapala2026Novel]. Small village tanks were constructed in linear series along headwater catchments, capturing seasonal runoff, trapping eroded sediments and recharging groundwater. Drainage from upper reservoirs fed secondary storage tanks downstream, which supplied water to communal paddy fields before excess flow drained into natural valley bottoms [@Abhayawardana2019Tank; @Sumanapala2026Novel].

From the first century AD onward, royal engineering scaled these local cascades into regional hydraulic networks [@Abeywardana2018Ancient; @Shannon2012Engineerin]. King Vasabha (65AD to 109AD) initiated the construction of twelve large reservoirs and trans-basin feeder canals. King Mahasena (274AD to 301AD) built the Minneriya tank, impounding 2.000 ha of water behind an earthen dam 13 metres high. King Dhatusena (459AD to 477AD) constructed the colossal Kalawewa and the 87 km Jaya Ganga (Yoda Ela), a trans-basin canal engineered at a gradient of less than ten centimetres per kilometre that transferred water from the Kala Oya basin to the urban reservoirs of Anuradhapura (Tissa Wewa, Nuwara Wewa) [@Abeywardana2019Evolution; @Muditha2026Hydraulic].

Central to these massive dams was the invention of the valve-pit (*bisokotuwa*) in the third century BC [@Muditha2026Hydraulic; @Uparathana2026Archaeolog]. This stone masonry rectangular shaft, set inside the upstream embankment face, acted as an energy dissipator, regulating hydraulic discharge through subterranean conduits while protecting earthen bunds from internal erosion and washouts [@Muditha2026Hydraulic]. Under Parakramabahu I (1153AD to 1186AD) at Polonnaruwa, the hydraulic system reached its structural apex with the construction of the Sea of Parakrama (Parakrama Samudra), a combined reservoir submerging 2.500 ha [@Abeywardana2018Ancient; @Shannon2012Engineerin]. Regional population attained its pre-colonial maximum of 1,95M inhabitants in 1200AD, with Rajarata supporting 585k people and Polonnaruwa housing 62k urban residents, succeeding Anuradhapura which had peaked at 90k inhabitants around 500AD [@Coningham2025Village; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade].

## The Thirteenth-Century Crisis and the Southwest Drift

The fourteenth century witnessed the collapse of the Rajarata hydraulic core and a decisive demographic realignment toward the southwest wet zone [@Manogaran1987Ethnic; @Coningham2025Village]. Multiple interacting pressures precipitated this contraction:
1. Destructive military invasions: repeated Chola and Pandyan incursions culminated in the devastating invasion of Kalinga Magha (1215AD to 1236AD), who looted monasteries and shattered the central administrative apparatus required to maintain regional sluices and canals [@DameronNandan2003World; @Coningham2025Village].
2. Hydroclimatic instability: speleothem and lake sediment proxies record erratic monsoon pulses, severe drought episodes and sudden catastrophic flooding during the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, breaching earthen bunds beyond local repair capacity [@Arachchige2021Multi; @Hewawasam2022Traditiona].
3. Malaria infestation: breaching of reservoirs and abandonment of canal maintenance transformed flowing waters into stagnant pools, facilitating the proliferation of vector mosquitoes (*Anopheles culicifacies*) and rendering the northern plains uninhabitable [@Manogaran1987Ethnic; @Kopke2023Human].
4. Geopolitical fragmentation: Sinhalese dynasts abandoned Polonnaruwa and retreated into defensive rock citadels and river valleys in the wet zone, moving the royal capital sequentially to Dambadeniya, Yapahuwa, Kurunegala, Gampola, Raigama and Kotte [@Coningham2025Village].

Simultaneously, the northern littoral consolidated under the independent Tamil kingdom of Jaffna (Nallur), governed by the Aryacakravarti dynasty, while the intervening forested tracts of the Vanni became autonomous chieftaincies paying nominal tribute [@Manogaran1987Ethnic; @Anthony2010Pastoral]. By 1500AD, regional population contracted to 1,55M inhabitants, with the southwest wet zone and Kandyan highlands housing 589k people (38% of the total) while Rajarata dropped to 465k.

## Early Modern Kingdoms and European Maritime Encroachment

During the sixteenth through eighteenth centuries, Sri Lanka's demographic landscape was shaped by the interplay between the interior Kandyan Kingdom and European colonial maritime powers [@Manogaran1987Ethnic; @Rakesh2020What]. In 1505AD, Portuguese fleets reached Colombo, establishing trading factories and fortified outposts to monopolise the island's lucrative wild cinnamon trade [@Green2025Indian; @Bohingamuwa2017Lanka]. By 1597AD, the Portuguese annexed the Kingdom of Kotte, followed by the conquest of the Jaffna Kingdom in 1619AD [@Anthony2010Pastoral].

In the central mountainous interior, the Kingdom of Kandy (Senkadagala) preserved its independence, leveraging rugged topography, tropical diseases and guerrilla tactics to repel multiple Portuguese invasions [@Manogaran1987Ethnic; @Kelegama2023Lure]. King Rajasinha II allied with the Dutch East India Company (VOC) to expel the Portuguese, culminating in the Dutch capture of Colombo in 1656AD and Jaffna in 1658AD [@Rakesh2020What].

Dutch rule (1658AD to 1796AD) transformed coastal demography. The VOC compiled systematic cadastral registers (*head-tombos* and *land-tombos*), drained coastal lagoons, developed canal networks linking Negombo, Colombo and Kalutara, and promoted cinnamon and coconut plantation agriculture [@Manogaran1987Ethnic]. By 1700AD regional population recovered to 1,75M, rising to 1,98M by 1796AD when British forces annexed Dutch maritime settlements during the Napoleonic wars.

## Atoll Ecology and the Maldivian Sultanate

The Maldives followed an insular demographic trajectory intimately connected to Indian Ocean maritime routes [@Clark2008Islands; @Feener2021Maldives]. Initial permanent settlement occurred during the early centuries AD by Indo-Aryan speakers migrating from Sri Lanka and western India, bringing Buddhism, advanced seafaring technology and the Dhivehi language [@Gippert2024Written; @Feener2021Maldives]. Archaeological excavations reveal monumental coral-stone Buddhist stupas (*havitta*) across southern atolls, notably at Fuvahmulah and Gan [@Feener2021Maldives].

In 1153AD, King Koimala converted to Islam, adopting the title Sultan Muhammad al-Adil [@Cui2025Religion; @Zahir2018Reformist]. The conversion anchored the Maldives firmly within Islamic maritime trading circuits linking the Persian Gulf, Red Sea, India and Southeast Asia [@Stosic2023Geopolitic; @Green2025Indian]. Maldivian cowrie shells served as official currency across Bengal, West Africa and China, while dried bonito (*maldive fish*) found eager markets in Sri Lanka and South India [@Zhang2023Chinese; @Eager2014Using].

Malé grew into a fortified political capital on an islet measuring less than two square kilometres, concentrating royal administration, court mosques and deep-water anchorages [@Feener2021Maldives; @MD2023Spatial]. Between 1000AD and 1796AD, Maldivian population expanded from 70k to 79,2k inhabitants, sustaining remarkable stability despite periodic Portuguese naval raids (1558AD to 1573AD) and French corsair incursions [@Cui2025Religion; @Zahir2018Reformist].

# Methodology

## Spatial Grid Configuration and Topographic Partitioning

The INDUS spatial framework partitions Sri Lanka and the Maldives archipelago across 768 active 5-arcminute terrestrial grid cells (representing 63.718 km²). Terrestrial surface evaluation combines environmental covariates:
- Orographic precipitation gradients: separating the southwest wet zone (annual precipitation 2.500 mm to 5.000 mm) from the seasonal dry zone (1.000 mm to 1.500 mm) [@Manogaran1987Ethnic; @Arachchige2021Multi].
- Fluvial network buffering: exponential distance decay from perennial trunk streams (Mahaweli, Kelani, Kalu) and seasonal dry zone rivers (Malvathu, Kala, Yan) [@Sutcliffe2011Historical].
- Karst limestone constraints: delimiting the Jaffna peninsula's freshwater lens and agricultural soil pockets [@Manogaran1987Ethnic].
- Coral atoll dry land: bounding the miniature island surfaces of the 26 Maldivian atolls to prevent spurious ocean cell allocation [@MD2023Spatial; @Feener2021Maldives].

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Surface Allocation

To prevent demographic double counting between nucleated urban centres and rural agrarian populations, 1.642 catalogued historical settlements are directly anchored to their WGS84 geographic coordinates [@Allchin1995Archaeology; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @ImperialGazetteer1908]. This expanded gazetteer integrates primary-monograph urban trajectories, multi-repository archaeological and monument corpora, national census schedules and macro-calibrated local administrative continuity (*nadu*, *pargana* and *qasba* market networks) filtered by documented foundation dates [@Habib1982Atlas; @Moosvi1987Economy; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade]. At each benchmark year, active populations of catalogued settlements are subtracted from their respective sub-regional envelopes.

The residual rural population is then dasymetrically distributed across non-settled grid cells in proportion to land suitability weights. Boundary feathering algorithms smooth density gradients across mountain divides and administrative limits, preventing step artefacts between adjacent river catchments.

## Demographic Uncertainty Bands

Every benchmark demographic estimate incorporates an explicit uncertainty envelope (+/- 14% to +/- 18% across prehistoric and classical epochs, tightening to +/- 12% in early modern periods). At the 1200AD peak, the regional total of 1,95M is bounded between 1,71M and 2,19M inhabitants. These intervals accommodate variations across competing historical estimates, house-mound densities and conflicting chronicle assertions [@Hawken2021Long; @Coningham2025Village].

# Testing and Validation

## Epigraphic and Textual Chronicle Corroboration

The demographic reconstructions are evaluated against Sri Lanka's extensive epigraphic and chronicle record [@Abeywardana2019Evolution; @DameronNandan2003World]. Over 4.000 published lithic inscriptions, beginning with third-century BC cave dedications in Early Brahmi script and continuing through mediaeval rock edicts and pillar inscriptions, record royal donations, tank ownership, water shares (*diyadada*) and monastic slave endowments [@Abeywardana2019Evolution; @Coningham2025Village].

The monastic chronicles, primarily the *Mahavamsa* and *Culavamsa*, provide continuous dynastic narratives chronicling reservoir construction, urban embellishments and agricultural colonisation projects [@DameronNandan2003World]. While chronicle descriptions of military levies and royal retinues contain conventional hyperbole, their records of specific reservoir foundations (e.g. Mahasena's sixteen tanks, Dhatusena's Kalawewa, Parakramabahu's canal schemes) correlate closely with physical masonry structures and stratified archaeological deposits [@Abeywardana2018Ancient; @Hawken2021Long].

In the Maldives, royal copperplate grants (*loamaafaanu*), engraved in ancient Eveyla Akuru and Dhives Akuru scripts from the late twelfth century AD onward, document mosque endowments, island tax rolls and conversion decrees, validating atoll settlement stability [@Gippert2024Written; @Feener2021Maldives].

## Geoarchaeology and Reservoir Siltation Chronologies

Geoarchaeological coring of reservoir sedimentary archives provides direct chronological constraints on agricultural intensity and landscape erosion [@Abeywardana2018Ancient; @Bebermeier2023Domesticat]. Sediment cores extracted from dry zone tanks (e.g. Nachchaduwa, Nuwara Wewa, Tissa Wewa) demonstrate low mineral sedimentation rates during early phases of tank construction, followed by marked increases in clay and silt deposition between 500AD and 1200AD, reflecting intensive watershed deforestation and double-crop paddy cultivation [@Abeywardana2018Ancient].

Pollen spectra preserved within tank silts indicate that scrub jungle was systematically cleared for wet-paddy and swidden (*chena*) cultivation, accompanied by managed agroforestry featuring coconut (*Cocos nucifera*), areca palm (*Areca catechu*) and jackfruit (*Artocarpus heterophyllus*) [@Bebermeier2023Domesticat; @Sumanapala2026Novel]. Radiocarbon dating of basal silt layers confirms that major reservoir bunds were continuously maintained until the late thirteenth century, after which coarse sandy washover deposits record unmaintained dam breaches and sediment bypass [@Abeywardana2018Ancient].

## Speleothem Paleoclimate Proxies and Monsoonal Variability

Paleoclimate records derived from speleothem oxygen isotope ratios ($\delta^{18}\text{O}$) and high-resolution marine sediment cores confirm the climatic forcing mechanisms driving regional agricultural fluctuations [@Arachchige2021Multi]. Stalagmite records from south-central Sri Lankan caves establish that the early first millennium AD experienced robust summer and winter monsoon rainfall, supporting the expansion of the Anuradhapura hydraulic network [@Arachchige2021Multi].

Between 950AD and 1150AD, precipitation remained high, facilitating the agricultural climax of the Polonnaruwa Kingdom. However, starting in the early thirteenth century, speleothem records document severe, protracted droughts punctuated by erratic mega-monsoon deluges [@Arachchige2021Multi; @Hewawasam2022Traditiona]. These climatic extremes placed unsustainable stress upon brittle canal networks, precipitating reservoir failures and accelerating the abandonment of the northern dry zone.

## Computational Fluid Dynamics and Valve-Pit Hydrodynamics

Recent engineering analyses of the ancient valve-pit (*bisokotuwa*) have demonstrated the sophisticated hydrodynamic principles underlying classical Sri Lankan dam construction [@Muditha2026Hydraulic]. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations conducted by Muditha and colleagues revealed that the bisokotuwa functioned as an effective kinetic energy dissipator [@Muditha2026Hydraulic].

By forcing high-pressure reservoir discharge into a rectangular stone chamber before routing it through paired masonry outflow culverts, the valve-pit reduced water velocity by over 60%, preventing erosion of downstream earthen bunds and eliminating hydraulic cavitation [@Muditha2026Hydraulic; @Uparathana2026Archaeolog]. This hydraulic stability enabled Sri Lankan engineers to construct dams exceeding 15 metres in height and impound storage volumes exceeding 50M m³, providing the caloric foundation for high dry zone population densities.

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The INDUS source ledger for Sri Lanka and the Maldives was compiled through a four-wave asymptotic ingestion process:
- Wave 1: Programmatic extraction from official national census schedules, primary-monograph metropolis anchors and heritage registries, incorporating 952 settlements [@ImperialGazetteer1908; @Bayly1983Rulers].
- Wave 2: Extraction from multi-repository archaeological and monument corpora (Pleiades, Zenodo regional inventories, ASI, Wikidata, OpenStreetMap and XRONOS/c14bazAAR), adding 460 settlements [@Allchin1995Archaeology; @Coningham2025Village].
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill, macro-calibrated pre-1800 *qasba*/*nadu* continuity and foundation-year toponymy audits, incorporating 230 settlements [@Habib1982Atlas; @Moosvi1987Economy; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making].
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap sweeps and GeoNames homonym audits across all five divisions (Rajarata 507, Kotte and wet zone 661, Ruhuna 304, Maldives 112 and Jaffna 58), yielding zero unaccounted settlements and confirming asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 1.872 candidate localities were audited: 1.642 were accepted as primary catalogued settlements and 230 were excluded (predominantly duplicate survey aliases within 2,2 km, toponymic homonyms or non-habitation features).

# Results

## Demographic Trajectory and Benchmark Analysis

The demographic history of Sri Lanka and the Maldives over eleven millennia demonstrates a trajectory characterised by steady prehistoric growth, a massive classical hydraulic urbanisation climax, a thirteenth-century structural relocation toward the southwest wet zone and Kandyan highlands, and early modern demographic recovery under maritime mercantilism (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

## Five Historical Demographic Epochs

### Terminal Pleistocene and Mesolithic Foragers (10000BC to 3000BC)

During the terminal Pleistocene and early Holocene, human populations in Sri Lanka were small, mobile hunting and gathering bands. Regional population was 12k in 10000BC (yielding an aggregate density of 0,19 persons per km² or 18,83 persons per 100 km²), rising to 65k by 3000BC (1,02 persons per km²). Settlement focused on wet zone rock shelters (Batadombalena, Kitulgala Beli-lena) and coastal sand dunes (Iranamadu Formation), where foragers exploited wild arboreal fauna, freshwater molluscs and coastal fisheries [@Clark2008Islands; @Coningham2025Village]. The Maldives remained uninhabited by sedentary communities, functioning as seasonal oceanic waypoints for maritime forager-fishers [@Clark2008Islands].

### Early Agro-Pastoral Settlement and Megalithic Horizons (3000BC to 500BC)

Between 3000BC and 500BC, sedentary village communities coalesced across the northern and eastern river plains [@Dissanayake2022Megalithic; @Abeywardana2019Evolution]. Population rose from 65k to 280k in 500BC (4,39 persons per km²). The introduction of iron smelting, black and red pottery, zebu cattle husbandry and small-scale earthen bund construction transformed human ecology. Megalithic burial cists in the Yan Oya valley document stratified pastoral-farming lineages managing local village tanks and ancestral cemeteries [@Dissanayake2022Megalithic]. By 500BC, early urban nucleations emerged at Anuradhapura along the Malvathu Oya and at Kantarodai on the Jaffna peninsula [@Coningham2025Village].

### The Classical Anuradhapura Hydraulic Era (500BC to 1000AD)

The millennium between 500BC and 1000AD represented the first sustained phase of urbanisation and demographic expansion [@Abeywardana2018Ancient; @Hawken2021Long]. Regional population expanded from 280k in 500BC to 650k by 0AD, 1,2M in 500AD and 1,75M by 1000AD (yielding an aggregate density of 27,47 persons per km²).

This growth was fueled by monumental royal hydraulic works [@Abeywardana2018Ancient; @Muditha2026Hydraulic]:
- Anuradhapura grew into a sprawling agro-urban metropolis covering over 40 km² across its monastic precincts (Mahavihara, Abhayagiri, Jetavana) and residential suburbs, housing 90k inhabitants at its 500AD peak [@Hawken2021Long; @Coningham2025Village; @Allchin1995Archaeology].
- Colossal reservoirs, including the Nuwara Wewa (1.200 ha), Tissa Wewa, Basawakkulama and Kalawewa, supplied perennial irrigation water to tens of thousands of hectares of double-cropped paddy fields [@Abeywardana2019Evolution].
- The port of Mantai (Mahatittha) on the northwestern coast operated as a cosmopolitan Indian Ocean emporium, reaching 24,9k inhabitants in 800AD and importing Roman coins, Persian ceramics, Chinese glazed wares and South Indian textiles in exchange for Sri Lankan gems, pearls and cinnamon [@Bohingamuwa2017Lanka; @Zhang2023Chinese].
- In the southeast, the principality of Ruhuna established an autonomous hydraulic core centred on Mahagama (Tissamaharama), supporting 28k residents at its 200AD peak and acting as a royal redoubt [@Coningham2025Village].

### Polonnaruwa Climax and Monumental Zenith (1000AD to 1200AD)

Following the Chola sack of Anuradhapura in 1017AD, King Vijayabahu I (1055AD to 1110AD) liberated the island and established the royal capital at Polonnaruwa, situated strategically near the Mahaweli River crossings [@DameronNandan2003World; @Coningham2025Village; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade]. Under Parakramabahu I (1153AD to 1186AD) and Nissanka Malla (1187AD to 1196AD), the kingdom attained its pre-colonial zenith, with regional population reaching 1,95M inhabitants in 1200AD (yielding an aggregate density of 30,6 persons per km²).

Polonnaruwa was fortified with triple brick walls, moats and monumental brick stupas (Rankoth Vehera, Hatadage), housing 62k urban inhabitants at its 1200AD zenith while Anuradhapura had contracted to 8k [@DameronNandan2003World; @Coningham2025Village]. The construction of the Sea of Parakrama (Parakrama Samudra), fed by the Angamedilla canal diverting the Amban Ganga, integrated three earlier reservoirs into a single inland sea impounding over 130M m³ of water [@Abeywardana2018Ancient; @Shannon2012Engineerin]. In the Maldives, conversion to Islam in 1153AD integrated the atolls into global trade circuits, with regional population expanding to 78k inhabitants [@Cui2025Religion; @Feener2021Maldives].

### Mediaeval Relocation, the Kandyan Kingdom and European Contact (1200AD to 1796AD)

Following the devastating invasion of Kalinga Magha in 1215AD, the dry zone hydraulic infrastructure suffered systemic collapse [@Manogaran1987Ethnic; @Coningham2025Village]. Sluices decayed, malaria infested the abandoned tank beds, and regional population contracted to 1,55M by 1500AD.

Sinhalese dynasts shifted their administrative capitals into the southwest wet zone: Dambadeniya (9,1k in 1300AD), Yapahuwa, Kurunegala, Gampola, Raigama and Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, which peaked at 42k inhabitants in 1450AD [@Coningham2025Village]. Rain-fed wet-paddy farming, terraced hill cultivation and spice harvesting replaced dry zone hydraulic agriculture [@Kelegama2023Lure].

In the north, the Tamil Kingdom of Jaffna consolidated under the Aryacakravartis in the late mediaeval Vijayanagara maritime orbit, peaking at 37,6k urban residents in 1600AD (and sustaining 34k by 1796AD), anchored by the royal precinct at Nallur (12k in 1600AD) and managing palmyra cultivation and pearl fisheries in the Gulf of Mannar [@Manogaran1987Ethnic; @Anthony2010Pastoral; @Stein1989Vijayanagara]. In the interior highlands, the Kingdom of Kandy emerged as a resilient bastion, peaking at 30k residents in 1700AD (28k in 1796AD) and developing terraced wet-rice farming and fortified mountain strongholds [@Manogaran1987Ethnic; @Kelegama2023Lure].

Following the arrival of the Portuguese (1505AD) and the Dutch (1658AD), coastal port towns and western wet zone market centres grew rapidly [@Green2025Indian; @Rakesh2020What; @Bayly1983Rulers]. Colombo expanded from a small Muslim trading roadstead (13,4k in 1200AD) into a fortified colonial capital housing 45k people by 1796AD, alongside Gampaha (35,9k), Galle (26k), Negombo (25,8k), Beruwala (25,5k) and Moratuwa (25,3k). Dutch canal construction, coconut cultivation and cinnamon plantation management fostered demographic recovery, with regional population reaching 1,75M in 1700AD and 1,98M by 1796AD on the eve of British annexation.

The urban settlement hierarchy conformed to a multi-tiered functional structure:
1. Primary metropolitan capitals (> 35k inhabitants): Anuradhapura (90k peak in 500AD), Polonnaruwa (62k peak in 1200AD), Colombo (45k in 1796AD), Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte (42k peak in 1450AD), Jaffna (37,6k peak in 1600AD) and Gampaha (35,9k in 1796AD). These centres directed state administration, religious ritual and foreign commercial exchange.
2. Major regional centres (20k to 35k inhabitants): Kandy (30k peak in 1700AD), Tissamaharama (28k peak in 200AD), Galle (26k in 1796AD), Negombo (25,8k in 1796AD), Beruwala (25,5k in 1796AD), Moratuwa (25,3k in 1796AD) and Mantai (24,9k peak in 800AD). These cities commanded primary river valleys, coastal fortresses and mountain passes.
3. Secondary specialised emporia, ports and provincial towns (10k to 20k inhabitants): Trincomalee (18k peak in 1650AD), Dambulla (15,6k in 1796AD), Batticaloa (15k in 1796AD), Sigiriya (12k peak in 500AD), Nallur (12k in 1600AD) and Malé (10,5k in 1796AD). These localities served as maritime customs ports, rock citadels, court precincts and naval bases.
4. Tertiary market towns and agricultural settlements (< 10k inhabitants): Kalpitiya (10k in 1796AD), Dambadeniya (9,1k in 1300AD), Pottuvil (7,3k in 1796AD), Kalmunai (6,2k in 1550AD), Kantarodai (5,9k in 1450AD) and over 1.600 agrarian villages, tank settlements and coral atoll communities distributed across the island and archipelago.

# Limitations

## Tropical Weathering and Archaeological Visibility

Archaeological investigations across Sri Lanka and the Maldives face severe preservation challenges [@Coningham2025Village; @Feener2021Maldives]:
1. Tropical humic soils and heavy monsoonal weathering: in the southwest wet zone, high annual rainfall (2.500 mm to 5.000 mm) and acidic lateritic soils dissolve bone collagen, wood and unbaked mud-brick architecture, leaving only stone foundations and ceramic scatters [@Coningham2025Village].
2. Dense jungle regrowth: following the mediaeval abandonment of Rajarata, tropical thorn scrub and monsoon forests engulfed ancient brick stupas and earthen bunds, obscuring site dimensions until twentieth-century forest clearance [@Abeywardana2018Ancient; @Fernando2011Current].
3. Modern urban overprinting: early historic strata beneath Colombo, Galle, Jaffna and Kandy are heavily disturbed by centuries of European colonial and modern commercial development, restricting excavations to salvage operations [@Coningham2025Village].
4. Coral atoll dynamic geomorphology: Maldivian coral islets undergo constant shoreline erosion, sand spit migration and storm-wave overwash, submerging or scattering ancient coastal settlements [@Feener2021Maldives; @MD2023Spatial].

## Epigraphic Monastic Biases

The vast majority of ancient Sri Lankan inscriptions record royal and elite donations of lands, irrigation shares and revenues to Buddhist monastic fraternities (Sangha) [@Abeywardana2019Evolution; @DameronNandan2003World]. While these texts provide invaluable evidence for land tenure, water rights and taxation, they disproportionately highlight monastic estates while leaving secular peasant hamlets and low-caste service villages under-documented [@Abeywardana2019Evolution; @Coningham2025Village].

## Malaria and the Collapse of Dry Zone Hydraulic Works

While traditional historiography attributed the collapse of Rajarata purely to Chola and Pandyan military invasions, modern ecological research emphasises the role of vector-borne malaria (*Plasmodium falciparum* and *Plasmodium vivax*) transmitted by *Anopheles culicifacies* [@Manogaran1987Ethnic; @Kopke2023Human]. The breach of storage embankments converted dynamic flowing canals into stagnant seepage pools, generating optimal breeding habitats for mosquitoes and rendering resettlement of the dry zone lethal until twentieth-century DDT eradication programmes [@Manogaran1987Ethnic].

## Insular Island Preservation and Sea-Level Fluctuations

In the Maldives, mid-Holocene sea-level fluctuations and limited island elevation (rarely exceeding two metres above mean sea level) restricted archaeological preservation [@Clark2008Islands; @Feener2021Maldives]. Calcareous coral stone, while durable, was frequently scavenged from pre-Islamic Buddhist stupas to construct mediaeval coral-stone mosques and tombs, recycling earlier architectural materials and confounding radiocarbon dating [@Gippert2024Written; @Feener2021Maldives].

# Conclusion

Sri Lanka and the Maldives sustained a demographic trajectory characterised by extraordinary hydraulic engineering, resilient insular trade networks and dramatic spatial realignments. From 12k terminal Pleistocene foragers in 10000BC, regional population expanded to 280k in 500BC with the establishment of Early Iron Age agro-pastoralism and tank irrigation. Under the classical kingdoms of Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa, the development of cascade reservoirs, trans-basin canals and energy-dissipating valve-pits enabled regional numbers to reach an all-time pre-colonial zenith of 1,95M inhabitants in 1200AD (yielding an aggregate density of 30,6 persons per km²).

The thirteenth-century collapse of the Rajarata hydraulic core was not an absolute demographic extinction, but an adaptive geographic relocation toward the rain-fed valleys of the southwest wet zone, the Kandyan montane massif, the Jaffna limestone shelf and the maritime trade corridors of the Indian Ocean. Rebounding to 1,98M by 1796AD, the island's demographic distribution on the eve of British rule established the geographic and urban framework that continues to define modern Sri Lanka and the Maldives today.
